abstract: Proposals to shorten the workweek are back on the policy agenda in Europe and the US. This column draws on France’s 35-hour reform to assess two central promises: work-sharing and productivity gains. In 2000, France cut the standard workweek from 39 to 35 hours at unchanged monthly pay and paired it with payroll tax cuts for employers. The authors find that the shorter workweek alone would have reduced employment by 4%, which the tax cuts fully offset. Productivity rose, but not enough to prevent a fall in output. Lower-skill workers bore most of the costs.
authors: Pauline Carry, Claire Montialoux, Elio Nimier-David, Alexandra Roulet, Nina Roussille
title: Shorter workweeks do not share work: Evidence from France's 35-hour reform

abstract: Cross-country data on what governments do are scarce. This column introduces the Global Fiscal Actions dataset, a new quarterly database of tax and spending measures in 142 countries since 1990, constructed using large language models to classify fiscal actions by their direction, instrument, motivation, implementation status, and size. Fiscal actions are frequent, typically small, predominantly expansionary, and spending-based, although fiscal sustainability is the most cited motivation. Over the past decade, spending actions have become less procyclical, while tax actions remain acyclical. Fiscal actions are synchronised across countries only during global recessions, and multipliers vary more within income groups than between them.
authors: Hites Ahir, Miyoko Asai, Matthieu Bellon, Maria Chiara Cavalleri, Shuvam Das, Davide Furceri, Faizaan Kisat, Aiko Mineshima, Irene Rausell Moreno, Vishal Parmar, Nikhil Patel, Adrian Peralta-Alva
title: Inside fiscal policy: A new dataset on government actions
